mcq.q: What is the most important difference between traditional apprenticeship and cognitive apprenticeship?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: Practice must be replaced by long lectures with many worked examples
All learning must move out of the classroom and into a real workshop
Thinking must be deliberately made visible
The number of learners per master must be cut so the master can stand by each one
mcq.e: The paper: "In apprenticeship, the processes of the activity are visible. In schooling, the processes of thinking are often invisible... Cognitive apprenticeship is a model of instruction that works to make thinking visible."

mcq.q: What are the four important aspects of traditional apprenticeship?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: Lecturing, drilling, testing and fading
Modeling, scaffolding, fading and coaching
Modeling, testing, ranking and grading
Observing, memorizing, copying and grading
mcq.e: "There are four important aspects of traditional apprenticeship: modeling, scaffolding, fading, and coaching."

mcq.q: What does modeling mean in traditional apprenticeship?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: The apprentice models the task for classmates to watch
The apprentice observes the master demonstrating parts of the task
The apprentice reads a manual before starting the work
The apprentice tries repeatedly and the master grades the result
mcq.e: "In modeling, the apprentice observes the master demonstrating how to do different parts of the task."

mcq.q: How is scaffolding described in the paper?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: A record of the apprentice's progress, week by week and skill by skill
A toolkit that the apprentice must buy and bring before entering the trade
An entrance test used to place apprentices in groups of suitable level
The master's support, from doing almost the whole task to giving occasional hints about what to do next
mcq.e: "Scaffolding is the support the master gives apprentices in carrying out a task. This can range from doing almost the entire task for them to giving occasional hints."

mcq.q: What is fading?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: Deleting hard content from the curriculum
Gradually reducing the number of exercises so the learner tires less
Gradually removing support so the learner takes on more responsibility
Gradually lowering the pass mark across tests
mcq.e: "Fading is the notion of slowly removing the support, giving the apprentice more and more responsibility."

mcq.q: Why is coaching called "the thread running through" the whole apprenticeship?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: The master chooses tasks, hints, diagnoses, encourages
The master works only with the best learner in the group
The master lectures at the start of the course and then leaves learners alone
The master appears only at the end to grade the finished product
mcq.e: "Coaching is the thread running through the entire apprenticeship experience... choosing tasks, providing hints and scaffolding, evaluating..., diagnosing..., challenging..., giving feedback."

mcq.q: What key role does Lave (1988) assign to observation?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: It helps learners build a conceptual model of the task before executing it
It lets the master judge learners faster in the first session
It helps learners remember the order of steps so they can copy them exactly
It lets learners avoid listening to the master's explanations
mcq.e: Observation "aids learners in developing a conceptual model of the target task prior to attempting to execute it."

mcq.q: What three reasons does the paper give for why a conceptual model (the big picture) helps in apprenticeship?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: It organizes first attempts, helps interpret the master's feedback
It helps memorization, copying and passing exams faster
It cuts cost, cuts time and cuts the number of people to supervise
It makes tasks easier, makes the master talk less, and raises marks
mcq.e: An advanced organizer for initial attempts; an interpretive structure for feedback and hints; an internalized guide during relatively independent practice.

mcq.q: What cognitive benefit does the social context of apprenticeship give?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: Learners are separated from the workplace so they can concentrate
Learners learn from a single master only, to avoid noise
Learners always see expert models at work, several masters
Learners never need to talk to anyone else
mcq.e: A community of practitioners shows there are multiple ways to do a task, that nobody holds all expertise, and that learning is an incrementally staged process.

mcq.q: What three differences separate traditional apprenticeship from cognitive apprenticeship?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: Drop modeling; drop coaching; drop fading from the whole teaching process
Use computers; use books; use video to replace the master's role entirely
Shorten learning time; cut costs; raise the number of learners each master handles
Make thinking visible; situate abstract tasks in real contexts
mcq.e: Teachers need to: (1) identify the processes of the task and make them visible; (2) situate abstract tasks in authentic contexts; (3) vary situations and articulate common aspects for transfer.

mcq.q: Why does traditional apprenticeship seldom face a need for skill transfer?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: Transfer is only for people with a university degree
The skills inhere in the task itself
Apprentices learn every skill of every trade
The work is repeated exactly the same way every day
mcq.e: "Skills to be learned inhere in the task itself... it is unlikely that students encounter situations in which the transfer of skills is required."

mcq.q: Do the authors claim cognitive apprenticeship is the only way to learn?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: No; books and lectures remain important
Yes, but only for the natural sciences
No; but reading and lectures are entirely useless
Yes; every other way of learning is rejected in the paper
mcq.e: "We do not want to argue that cognitive apprenticeship is the only way to learn. Reading a book or listening to a lecture are important ways to learn."

mcq.q: Why do passive readers and listeners learn less, per the paper?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: Apprenticeship forces learners to use their knowledge, whereas passive reading
They do not have enough time in class to read and listen to everything offered
They do not like the subject, so they pay less attention than other learners
Books and lectures always contain many more errors than real practical work does
mcq.e: "To the degree that readers or listeners are passive, however, they will not learn as much as they would by apprenticeship, because apprenticeship forces them to use their knowledge."

mcq.q: In the conclusion, for what kind of goal do the authors say cognitive apprenticeship is NOT suitable?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: A complex task such as proving a mathematical theorem in several steps
A task such as comprehending a difficult text with several layers of meaning
A rote task such as French verb conjugation or the elements of the periodic table
A task such as writing a reasoned opinion essay with a clear thesis
mcq.e: "It does not make sense to use it to teach the rules of conjugation in French or to teach the elements of the periodic table... useful when a teacher needs to teach a fairly complex task."

mcq.q: What do the authors say about the teacher's role as "expert"?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: Only the best teachers may act as experts
It is not fixed; the expert
The teacher keeps the expert role for the whole course
Students may never challenge the teacher's solutions
mcq.e: "Cognitive apprenticeship encourages the student to become the expert."

mcq.q: What does the paper say about a formula for applying cognitive apprenticeship?
mcq.sec: Collins, Brown & Holum 1991: the core idea
o: There is a fixed five-step formula for every subject
There is a formula prescribed by the education ministry
There is a formula but usable only for three foundation subjects
There is none; teachers find ways to apply it in their own domain
mcq.e: "We don't believe that there is a formula... Ultimately, it is up to the teacher to identify ways in which cognitive apprenticeship can work in his or her own domain."

mcq.q: Which four skills does Palincsar and Brown's (1984) reciprocal teaching teach?
o: Speed reading, underlining, note-taking and testing
Guessing meaning, using a dictionary, translating and comparing
Reading aloud, dictation, memorizing and paraphrasing
Questioning, summarizing, predicting
mcq.e: "formulating questions based on the text, summarizing the text, making predictions about what will come next, and clarifying difficulties with the text."

mcq.q: Why is it called "reciprocal" teaching?
o: Teacher and students take turns playing the role of teacher
Students teach the whole content back at the end of term
Two students swap their work to grade it
The teacher and parents teach together
mcq.e: "It is called reciprocal teaching because the teacher and students take turns playing the role of teacher."

mcq.q: For whom was reciprocal teaching originally designed?
o: Older adults learning a foreign language
Kindergarten children who do not yet know letters
Middle-school students who decode adequately
University students writing dissertations
mcq.e: "originally designed for middle school students who could decode adequately but had serious comprehension problems; it can be adapted to any age group."

mcq.q: How many students per group is reciprocal teaching used with?
o: Ten to twenty students
A whole class of forty at once
Two to seven students
Exactly three students, no more
mcq.e: "used with groups of two to seven students, as well as individual students."

mcq.q: What happened to poor readers' comprehension scores in the pilot with individual students?
o: Rose from 50% to 55% accuracy after about thirty sessions
Rose from 30% to 60% accuracy after about two sessions
Rose from 15% to 85% accuracy after about twenty sessions
Rose from 40% to 80% accuracy after about five sessions
mcq.e: Six months later they were at 60%; one session was enough to get back to 85%.

mcq.q: What happened with groups of two students?
o: Scores fell from 80% to 30%, dropping a lot after eight weeks
Scores rose from about 30% to 80%
Scores went from 40% to 45%, unchanged after eight weeks
Scores rose from 15% to 85%, dropping a lot after eight weeks
mcq.e: "the scores increased from about 30 percent to 80 percent accuracy, with very little change eight weeks later."

mcq.q: What happened with classroom groups of four to seven students?
o: Scores rose from 15% to 85%, unchanged after eight weeks
Scores rose from about 40% to 80%
Scores went from 60% to 65%, declining steeply after eight weeks
Scores fell from 80% to 40%, declining steeply after eight weeks
mcq.e: The authors call these "very dramatic effects for any instructional intervention."

mcq.q: What four factors explain the success of reciprocal teaching?
o: A new conceptual model of reading
New textbooks; projectors; tests; gifts
Short texts; long lessons; bonus points; end-of-term prizes
Memorization; repetition; copying; frequent testing
mcq.e: The four factors in the authors' analysis: conceptual model, modeling with comparison, scaffolding, producer and critic roles.

mcq.q: How does the dual "producer and critic" role help students?
o: They must grade their peers so that the teacher has less marking to do
They must state what makes a good question or summary
They must work faster without stopping to think about the quality of the work
They must memorize the text more exactly so they can answer any question
mcq.e: Evaluating others' products forces students to articulate their knowledge of quality; it is then freed from its contextual binding and usable in many contexts.

mcq.q: What is "knowledge telling" per Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987)?
o: The novice writer's strategy: write the first idea, then the next
Copying passages verbatim from reference material and stitching them together
Reading the finished piece aloud to the class and taking their comments
The expert's strategy: plan the piece and revise it many times before finishing
mcq.e: This simple control strategy finesses most of the difficulties in composing.

mcq.q: What is "knowledge transforming"?
o: A way of writing as fast as possible in order to meet a deadline
The expert process that combines linear text generation with goal setting
A way of copying knowledge word for word from a textbook into one's own notes
A way of translating a piece of writing into another language without losing meaning
mcq.e: Experts spend time not only writing but also planning and revising (Hayes and Flower 1980).

mcq.q: Into how many processes did Scardamalia and Bereiter break planning, and which?
o: Three: introduction, body, conclusion
Five: new idea, improve an idea, elaborate an idea
Four: choose a topic, find sources, write, submit
Six: read, take notes, copy, summarize, revise, submit
mcq.e: (a) generating a new idea, (b) improving an idea, (c) elaborating on an idea, (d) identifying goals, (e) putting ideas into a cohesive whole.

mcq.q: What kind of support are Scardamalia and Bereiter's cue cards?
o: A spelling guide written for people who are just beginning to write
A reward system meant to encourage students to write more in every session
Procedural facilitation: opening phrases students choose from
A mark sheet kept for each student to compare results across the whole class
mcq.e: Examples: "An even better idea is...", "I'm not being very clear about what I just said so...".

mcq.q: What is "soloing" in the writing method?
o: A student plans a new essay alone with cue cards while the teacher
A student sings alone in front of the whole class to build self-confidence
A student writes a piece in which no topic was given in advance
A student sits a test on their own without being allowed the cue cards
mcq.e: After the teacher models it, each student plans an essay on a new topic; the teacher and other students evaluate the soloist's performance.

mcq.q: What did the study of revision (Bereiter and Scardamalia 1987) find?
o: Idea-level revisions only doubled
No support had an effect by itself
Combined supports gave better revisions
Revisions rose tenfold but stylistic quality fell sharply
mcq.e: "a tenfold increase in the frequency of idea-level revisions, without any decrease in stylistic revisions."

mcq.q: In the planning study (Scardamalia et al. 1984), how did planning time change?
o: It halved, yet the experimental students' texts were still judged better
It doubled, but only among the strongest students in each classroom
It rose tenfold, and experimental students' texts were judged better in thought content
It stayed unchanged, and the two groups' texts were judged equal in quality
mcq.e: There was also more reflective activity even when the prompts were no longer available.

mcq.q: Why is it useful for students to see the teacher struggle in live modeling?
o: It makes students dislike writing
It saves the teacher preparation time
It shows that writing is not the smooth
It leads students to lose respect for the teacher
mcq.e: Students rarely see writers at work so hold naive beliefs; live modeling shows struggles, false starts and discouragement.

mcq.q: On what does Schoenfeld (1985) base his teaching of problem solving to college students?
o: Doing many identical problems until the solution method is known by heart
Memorizing every formula in the textbook so it can be used on demand
Heuristic strategies derived from Polya (1945), plus control strategies
Copying the teacher's model solutions and reusing them on new problems
mcq.e: A heuristic is a rule of thumb: try n = 1, 2, 3, 4 and induce; for geometry examine minimal cases such as regular polygons or right triangles.

mcq.q: What are "control strategies" according to Schoenfeld?
o: Rules about the time allowed and how solutions must be laid out
Exact calculation formulas used for each particular type of problem
Ways of grading work against a marking scheme set by the teacher
Executive decisions: generating alternatives, evaluating them
mcq.e: "control strategies are concerned with executive decisions, such as generating alternative courses of action, evaluating which will get you closer to a solution..." Schoenfeld found both heuristics and control strategies must be taught.

mcq.q: What is the "polynomials with reversed coefficients" problem used for in the paper?
o: To prove Fermat's last theorem through a series of complicated derivations
To show a mathematician thinking aloud: try simple examples, conjecture
To teach students to solve quadratic equations with the standard formula
To test how quickly students can calculate when faced with a new problem
mcq.e: The finding: the roots of P and Q are reciprocals; the terse final proof hides two breakthroughs that a postmortem reveals.

mcq.q: What two "breakthroughs" does Schoenfeld identify in the polynomial problem?
o: Copying the solution of an old problem; then changing the numbers to fit
Understanding the problem by trying easy-to-calculate examples for a pattern
Using a calculator to try many cases; then asking the teacher whether it is right
Guessing the answer from the form of the problem; then checking by substitution
mcq.e: Breakthrough 1: choose easily factorable examples to spot a pattern. Breakthrough 2: after conjecturing, go back and ask "what does it mean for r to be a root?"

mcq.q: Why does Schoenfeld offer to solve hard problems students bring?
o: So they see experts struggle
To prove he can always solve any problem
So students can copy the solution after class
To test the students' knowledge
mcq.e: Textbook solutions show only the successful path, not the search space with dead ends.

mcq.q: In small groups, what three questions does Schoenfeld ask as a "consultant"?
o: Who is doing it, where, and when is it due
What are they doing, why, and how will it help them find a solution
Do they understand the task, do they need help, and which group is better
Are they done, is it right, and how long did it take
mcq.e: These questions promote reflection, self-monitoring and articulating reasons; students come to ask them of themselves, so the teacher is fading.

mcq.q: What four reasons does Schoenfeld give for small-group problem solving?
o: Coaching during semi-independent solving; discussion clarifies control
Preventing cheating; avoiding noise; avoiding lateness; avoiding absence
Saving paper; reducing marking; raising class size; creating competition
Raising marks; cutting time; adding prizes; reducing pressure
mcq.e: The teacher cannot coach effectively on homework; choosing among methods provokes articulation; students get little chance to collaborate; seeing peers struggle reduces insecurity.

mcq.q: Which three roles in complex problem solving do small groups differentiate and externalize?
o: Moderator (executive), generator of alternatives
Leader, follower and observer, each staying in the same role throughout
Questioner, answerer and marker who each check the others' work
Reader of the task, calculator and note-taker in a fixed rotation
mcq.e: Students can rotate roles to practise all activities they need to internalize.

mcq.q: What is "postmortem analysis" (abstracted replay) in Schoenfeld's method?
o: Totalling the cost of running the class over the whole term
Recounting the solution and highlighting generalizable features: heuristics, decision points, reasons for choices
Reading the task one last time before it is handed in for marking
Marking the work in order to rank the students within the whole class
mcq.e: Alternating expert and student postmortems lets the class compare, diagnose difficulties and make incremental adjustments.

mcq.q: What are the four dimensions of a learning environment in the Collins, Brown and Holum framework?
o: Time, space, cost and people
Teachers, students, materials and facilities
Goals, plans, implementation and evaluation
Content, method, sequence and sociology
mcq.e: "content, method, sequence, and sociology."

mcq.q: What are the four types of knowledge in the "content" dimension?
o: Domain knowledge, heuristic strategies, control strategies
Theory, practice, revision and testing, in the order they are taught
Facts, dates, names and places gathered from the whole textbook
Reading, writing, speaking and listening, the four basic language skills
mcq.e: Domain knowledge, heuristic strategies, control strategies, learning strategies.

mcq.q: What is domain knowledge, and what is its limitation when learned in isolation?
o: Rules of thumb; always correct
New learning strategies; always usable at once
Concepts, facts and procedures of the subject
Time-management methods; always useful
mcq.e: "when it is learned in isolation from realistic problem contexts... domain knowledge tends to remain inert." Examples in reading: vocabulary, syntax, phonics rules.

mcq.q: Which is an example of a heuristic strategy?
o: In reading: remember the meaning of "meticulous"
In writing: plan to rewrite the introduction
In history: know the year of an event
In math: know the quadratic formula
mcq.e: Heuristics are "tricks of the trade" that do not always work; in math: find a solution for simple cases and see if it generalizes.

mcq.q: Which is an example of a control strategy?
o: Remember a new word's meaning with a rhyme so that it sticks in memory
Copy the whole passage out by hand so that it is easier to remember
Read fast in order to get through the passage as soon as possible
Try to state the main point of what you just read; if you cannot
mcq.e: Control strategies have monitoring, diagnostic and remedial components; in math: switch to a new part of the problem if stuck.

mcq.q: Which example of "learning strategies" is given?
o: Do the homework in the evening so as not to pile the work up before a deadline
Learn the lesson by heart in the evening just before going to sleep
Relate each step of a textbook example to the principles in the text (Chi et al. 1989)
Read the material in the quietest voice possible so as not to disturb others
mcq.e: They also include finding people to critique your writing with reasons, and analysing others' texts for strengths and weaknesses.

mcq.q: What are the six teaching methods in the framework and how are they grouped?
o: Modeling, coaching, scaffolding; articulation, reflection
Reading, writing, speaking, listening, doing, remembering (one group)
Listening, looking, doing, testing, marking, ranking (two groups)
Lecturing, asking, answering, testing, commenting, correcting (three groups)
mcq.e: The first three are the core of cognitive apprenticeship; articulation and reflection focus observation and give conscious access to one's own strategies; exploration encourages autonomy.

mcq.q: Which example illustrates modeling in reading?
o: A teacher copies the passage onto the board for the class to read together
A teacher reads very fast so that the whole class can follow the sound
A teacher hands out a passage and stays silent while students work alone
A teacher reads aloud in one voice while verbalizing thought processes in another
mcq.e: Collins and Smith (1982). In math, Schoenfeld models by solving hard problems students bring to class.

mcq.q: What does coaching mean in the framework?
o: Copying lecture notes on the board
Observing students perform
A final exam followed by marking
Lecturing theory at the start of a session
mcq.e: Coaching content relates directly to specific events as the student attempts the task; it can remind of something known but temporarily overlooked.

mcq.q: What is required for scaffolding?
o: Many similar exercises
Accurate diagnosis of current skill
A detailed score sheet for the whole class
A textbook shared by the whole school
mcq.e: Examples: cue cards for writing, or short skis for teaching skiing (Burton, Brown and Fisher 1984).

mcq.q: Which ways of articulation does the framework include?
o: Inquiry teaching, encouraging thinking aloud while solving
Watching films, listening to music and playing games to relax after class
Copying lines many times, sitting a final exam, and being ranked in class
Silent reading, note-taking, and handing the work in for the teacher to mark
mcq.e: Inquiry teaching (Collins and Stevens 1982, 1983) is questioning to get students to articulate and refine understanding, e.g. why one summary is good and another poor.

mcq.q: What is reflection in the framework?
o: Sitting and thinking about the task all day without comparing with anyone
Comparing one's own process with an expert's or another student's
Rereading the teacher's notes in order to correct mistakes in the work
Grading oneself against the mark scheme that the teacher provides
mcq.e: An abstracted replay highlights the critical features; for example recording students thinking aloud and replaying it for comparison.

mcq.q: What is exploration and why is it the endpoint of fading?
o: Taking students on a field trip
Letting students rest after a lesson
Having students redo old tasks
Pushing students to solve
mcq.e: Examples: send students to the library to investigate why the stock market crashed in 1929; write an essay defending the most outrageous thesis.

mcq.q: What are the three principles of the "sequencing" dimension?
o: Easy before hard; short before long; old before new
Global before local skills; increasing complexity; increasing diversity
Theory before practice; lecture before exercises; example before task
Reading before writing; listening before speaking; understanding before doing
mcq.e: Global before local skills; increasing complexity; increasing diversity.

mcq.q: Which example illustrates "global before local" in tailoring apprenticeship?
o: Apprentices assemble a garment from pre-cut pieces before learning to cut the pieces
Apprentices embroider complex patterns before learning basic stitches
Apprentices measure people precisely before seeing a finished pattern
Apprentices learn to cut fabric expertly before knowing what the garment looks like
mcq.e: Lave (1988): build a conceptual map before attending to details; in algebra, students are relieved of low-level computation to concentrate on higher-order reasoning.

mcq.q: By which two mechanisms is "increasing complexity" managed?
o: More exercises each day; less explanation from the teacher during lessons
Longer time to complete the test; fewer questions so students have time to think
Sequencing tasks to control complexity; using scaffolding
Higher bonus marks for hard tasks; less pressure from the final exam
mcq.e: Example from tailoring: first make drawers (straight lines, few pieces), then blouses (curved lines, pockets, collar).

mcq.q: When does "increasing diversity" matter?
o: Once a skill is well learned
When the teacher is absent, give easy tasks
When students are bored, change subject
When the skill is unknown, repeat one type of task
mcq.e: Diversity builds a richer network of contextual associations, so strategies are available for novel problems; in reading: pleasure, study and information-seeking reading.

mcq.q: What are the four characteristics of the "sociology" dimension?
o: Situated learning
Class size, hours, timetable, room
Discipline, marks, exams, ranking
Power, money, fame, scholarships
mcq.e: Situated learning, community of practice, intrinsic motivation, exploiting cooperation.

mcq.q: What are the four purposes of situated learning per the paper?
o: Understand uses of knowledge; learn by active use
Get to know the teacher; classmates; school; timetable
Go on trips; take photos; take notes; hand in reports
Save paper; reduce noise; reduce time; raise marks
mcq.e: Knowledge acquired has a dual form, tied to contexts and independent of them; "unbinding" fosters transfer. Dewey had students design and build a clubhouse.

mcq.q: What is the nature of a community of practice per the paper?
o: It can only appear among experts who have many years of experience behind them
It can only arise through competition on marks between groups in the class
It can be created by school regulation and checked regularly by inspectors
It cannot be forced but can be fostered by common projects
mcq.e: A community leads to a sense of ownership, personal investment and mutual dependency.

mcq.q: What is an example of intrinsic motivation in reading and writing?
o: Students reading a textbook to please the class teacher
Students writing an essay to get high marks in the end-of-term exam
Students copying a friend's work to hand in on time
Students communicating by e-mail with students elsewhere in the world
mcq.e: Lepper and Greene (1979), Malone (1981): working because the task is tied to an interesting goal, not for extrinsic reasons like marks.

mcq.q: What is the central claim of Brown, Collins and Duguid (1989)?
o: Knowledge is abstract and can be fully separated from the situation of learning
Knowledge is situated, in part a product of the activity, context
Knowledge exists only in each individual's head
Knowledge can be learned only from textbooks
mcq.e: "knowledge is situated, being in part a product of the activity, context, and culture in which it is developed and used."

mcq.q: Which assumption of many teaching practices does the paper criticize?
o: That teachers need a solid command of the subject to teach it
That classrooms need textbooks and reference material to work properly
That students need inner motivation in order to learn anything well
That conceptual knowledge can be abstracted from the situations in
mcq.e: The split between "know what" and "know how" may be a product of the structure and practices of the education system.

mcq.q: What did Miller and Gildea (1987) study about vocabulary?
o: Children taught words from pictures and videos
Children taught words from computer games
Children taught words from dictionary definitions
Children taught words from competitions between classes
mcq.e: Learning outside school is fast and successful; from abstract definitions it is slow and generally unsuccessful.

mcq.q: What is the rate of vocabulary learning of a 17-year-old outside school compared with in class?
o: About 5,000 words a year (13 a day)
About 1,000 words a year with both methods
About 500 words a year, versus about 5,000 a year in class
About 50 words a year, versus about 500 a year in class
mcq.e: "the average 17-year-old has learned vocabulary at a rate of 5,000 words per year (13 per day) for over 16 years... barely enough classroom time to teach more than 100 to 200 words per year."

mcq.q: What does the sentence "Me and my parents correlate, because without them I wouldn't be here" illustrate?
o: A pupil who has deeply understood the word correlate and uses it accurately
A pupil misuses a word learned from definitions without normal context of use
A pupil deliberately joking with the teacher to lighten the mood in class
A pupil who does not know basic English grammar and so writes wrong sentences
mcq.e: Teaching from dictionaries treats definitions and sentences as self-contained "pieces", ignoring extralinguistic support.

mcq.q: What are indexical words such as I, here and now?
o: Words borrowed from another language and not yet fully naturalized
Words that "point" to part of the communicative situation
Words with several different meanings listed in the large dictionaries
Words used only in formal writing and never in ordinary speech
mcq.e: Brown et al. argue that nearly all words are at least partly indexical (Barwise and Perry 1983).

mcq.q: Why do phone discussions of a paper make indexical terms a problem?
o: Because the speaker does not remember the paper and must describe it again at length
Because the phone line has noise, so the listener cannot hear clearly
The listener lacks the shared situation to interpret "here" or "this"
Because indexical terms are banned in serious academic writing
mcq.e: "Descriptions are at best translucent and at worst opaque"; the more elaborate a description to avoid ambiguity, the more opaque it may become.

mcq.q: What does treating concepts as "tools" imply?
o: Concepts are only for experts who have spent many years studying them
Concepts cannot change over time whatever the activity in which they are used
You can hold a tool and not know how to use it
Concepts can always be bought in a shop and used straight away by anyone
mcq.e: Example: the pocket-knife device for removing stones from horses' hooves; its owner may talk wisely about horses but not know how to use it on a limping horse.

mcq.q: Carpenters and cabinet makers use chisels differently. What does this illustrate?
o: How a tool is used reflects the community and its view of the world
All craftsmen use tools in exactly the same way whichever community they belong to
Tools can only be used in a workshop and never anywhere else
A good tool has only one correct way of being used, whoever the user is
mcq.e: "the community and its viewpoint, quite as much as the tool itself, determine how a tool is used." Activity, concept and culture are interdependent.

mcq.q: According to the paper, what is learning?
o: A process of enculturation
A process of testing and marking
A process of competition between individuals
A process of continuous memorization of information
mcq.e: "learning is, we believe, a process of enculturation." People continually adopt the behaviour and belief systems of new social groups.

mcq.q: How is "authentic" activity defined in the paper?
o: Tasks only experts can do
Activities graded by the school
The ordinary practices of the culture
The hardest exercises in the textbook
mcq.e: "Authentic activities then, are most simply defined as the ordinary practices of the culture." Novices such as apprentice tailors ironing garments also do authentic activity.

mcq.q: Why does the paper call much school activity "ersatz"?
o: Because teachers lack expertise
Because students are not serious
Because schools lack equipment
When brought into class
mcq.e: This "hybrid" activity is framed by school culture but attributed to the culture of readers, mathematicians and historians. Success in it often has little bearing on performance elsewhere.

mcq.q: How does the paper characterize textbook word problems?
o: Very close to the practice of working mathematicians in their daily work
Present only in modern textbooks from the last few decades
Always loved by students because they connect with everyday life
Encoded in a syntax common only to other math problems
mcq.e: The word problems of a textbook of 1478 are instantly recognizable today (Lave 1988c).

mcq.q: How do JPFs (just plain folks), students and practitioners differ in Table 1?
o: JPFs reason with causal stories; students with laws
JPFs with formulas; students with stories; practitioners with laws
All three with laws
All three with stories
mcq.e: Table 1: reasoning with: causal stories (JPF), laws (students), causal models (practitioners); acting on: situations, symbols, conceptual situations; meaning: negotiable, fixed, negotiable.

mcq.q: What kind of problems does each group resolve in Table 1?
o: JPFs: ill-defined; students: emergent; practitioners: well-defined
JPFs: emergent problems; students: well-defined problems
All three groups solve emergent problems
All three groups solve well-defined problems
mcq.e: Emergent problems and dilemmas (JPF), well-defined problems (students), ill-defined problems (practitioners).

mcq.q: What does the Weight Watchers example (Lave 1988) illustrate?
o: A dieter solves "three-quarters of two-thirds of a cup" with the cup
The dieter has to relearn his school maths before he can do the task
The dieter always uses a pocket calculator to multiply two fractions
The dieter does not know how to multiply fractions so he measures by eye
mcq.e: He poured two-thirds of a cup on a board, patted it into a circle, marked a cross and removed a quadrant: problem, solution and procedure coincided; no paper-and-pencil check.

mcq.q: What does Scribner's (1984) example of dairy loaders show?
o: Workers always use an electronic calculator placed in the depot to add up
Workers do complex calculations by using the configuration of crates as an elaborate abacus
Workers need not calculate anything because someone has calculated it already
Workers must learn the multiplication table thoroughly before starting work
mcq.e: Cognition is distributed across the social and physical environment; Hutchins studied naval navigation with similar distribution.

mcq.q: What does it mean when students rely on cues such as "first end-of-chapter questions are easy"?
o: Students are cheating in tests by looking at the work of their neighbours
Students have a special talent for maths and so guess the question correctly
Students are lazy and just look for the fastest way to copy the answer
Students remain situated: they lean on any available context
mcq.e: Schoenfeld: a problem's position in the chapter, or the word "left" signalling subtraction. Effective in school but "extremely fragile" outside.

mcq.q: Why might school disregard students' inventive heuristics?
o: Because those heuristics are all wrong and would lead students astray
Because textbooks do not allow any method other than the one they teach
Because teachers have never actually seen students using those heuristics
It accepts only the "standard" solution
mcq.e: Lave (1988c) describes students disguising effective strategies.

mcq.q: What does the paper say about the difference between plans and situated actions?
o: Plans are always more accurate than actions in every situation
They are identical because a plan always predicts the action exactly
Actions can always be fully replaced by a detailed written description
They differ; a manual's picture differs from the real machine
mcq.e: Suchman (1987): representations arising from activity cannot easily (or perhaps at all) be replaced by descriptions.

mcq.q: Why does the paper say knowledge is "spread" like a jigsaw picture?
o: Because knowledge is an image
Because jigsaw pieces help children learn
Because part is in the mind
Because games should be used in class
mcq.e: Cognition is widely distributed across the social and physical environment (Hutchins, Pea).

mcq.q: What implication for teaching methods follows from the indexicality of knowledge?
o: Situated methods are only one optional choice among many for the teacher
A well-written textbook is all that is needed for students to learn well
Only the strongest students need to be taught, and the rest will follow
Learning methods embedded in authentic situations are not merely useful
mcq.e: "learning methods that are embedded in authentic situations are not merely useful; they are essential."

mcq.q: In Schoenfeld's class, why did they not stop when the magic square problem had an answer?
o: Because the problem statement had not finished printing so they had to wait
The goal was to understand the mathematical nature of the problem
Because the answer was wrong so the class had to start again from scratch
Because there was spare time so the teacher gave extra work to fill it
mcq.e: In ordinary classes a "problem" is an exercise showing mastery by getting the answer; Schoenfeld answered "no".

mcq.q: Which strategies did Schoenfeld's class draw out of the magic square problem?
o: Guessing the answer; asking friends; waiting for the teacher; checking
Memorizing; repeating; copying; handing in
Cheating; copying; skipping; asking for marks
Focusing on key points that give leverage; exploiting extreme cases
mcq.e: The strategies were illustrated in action, developed by the class, not declared by the teacher.

mcq.q: Where did Lampert (1986) begin teaching multiplication to fourth graders?
o: With an end-of-term test to find out how much students had already learned
With the multiplication table, since it underlies every later multiplication
With the standard multi-digit algorithm so students meet it early
With coin problems, because the class community has a shared implicit understanding of coins
mcq.e: An example task: "using only nickels and pennies, make 82 cents".

mcq.q: What are the three phases of Lampert's multiplication teaching?
o: Coin problems; students create stories for multiplication
Read the chapter; listen to the lecture; then take notes on it
Watch a video; see a demonstration; then hand in the completed work
Memorize; do exercises; then take a test to check the result
mcq.e: The standard algorithm is presented as one more useful strategy for resolving the community's problems.

mcq.q: What four kinds of mathematical knowledge does Lampert's method combine?
o: Intuitive, computational, concrete
Reading, writing, listening and speaking
Theory, practice, revision and testing
Memorizing, understanding, applying and creating
mcq.e: Intuitive, computational, concrete, principled (associativity, commutativity); the aim is inseparable understanding, bridging knowing and doing.

mcq.q: What is the main difference between Schoenfeld's and Lampert's approaches per the paper?
o: Lampert teaches only university classes while Schoenfeld teaches only young children
The two approaches are identical in every goal and every method they use
Schoenfeld more strongly stresses exposing students to a culture's authentic ways of thinking and its conceptual viewpoint
Schoenfeld teaches only algorithms while Lampert teaches only stories
mcq.e: "Schoenfeld's approach differs principally in its strong emphasis on exposing students to the authentic ways of thinking of a culture."

mcq.q: Whom did Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976) study, and with what task?
o: 309 eleventh graders solving physics problems about moving vehicles
30 children aged 3, 4, 5 (10 per age) building a 21-block pegged wooden pyramid
60 ninth graders solving statistics problems about standard deviation
24 tenth graders solving trigonometry problems under a dual-task condition
mcq.e: Each age group was split equally by sex; recruited through advertisements, mainly middle-class families; sessions 20 minutes to 1 hour.

mcq.q: How many blocks and levels did the pyramid have?
o: 30 blocks, ten levels, about 20 inches high
8 blocks, two levels, about 3 inches high
21 blocks, six levels, about 9 inches high
12 blocks, three levels, about 5 inches high
mcq.e: The top block was solid; each remaining layer was four blocks formed of two locking pairs with peg and hole fittings.

mcq.q: What was the main rule for the tutor's teaching in the study?
o: Stay silent and never intervene
Always do it for the child to finish quickly
Let the child do as much as possible
Always ask for the final answer
mcq.e: "her aim with every child was to allow him to do as much as possible for himself." The next level of instruction depended on the child's success or failure.

mcq.q: How does the paper describe its own status regarding hypotheses?
o: A survey of parents' opinions
A precise experiment testing a stated hypothesis with a control group
A systematic description of how children respond to forms of aid
A literature review
mcq.e: "Our observations are not to be regarded as a test of an hypothesis about the tutoring process."

mcq.q: What was the inter-scorer reliability in the study?
o: 94% agreement on 594 events scored from videotape
100% agreement on 30 events scored from teaching sessions
60% agreement on 100 events scored from handwritten notes
75% agreement on 1,000 events scored from audio tapes
mcq.e: Two scorers worked independently.

mcq.q: What is the key condition for a learner to benefit from a tutor's help?
o: Comprehension (recognizing the solution) must precede production
Production (making the solution) must come before comprehension (recognizing it)
Comprehension and production are completely independent and unrelated
The tutor only needs to praise the learner often for the learner to progress
mcq.e: "comprehension of the solution must precede production", because without it there can be no effective feedback.

mcq.q: What did the 3-year-olds show about recognition and production?
o: As good at both producing and recognizing as 5-year-olds
Unable to recognize anything
Able to produce but not to recognize
Far worse at building correct assemblies
mcq.e: 3-year-olds reassembled two-thirds of correct constructions they took apart but only 14% of incorrect ones. None reassembled incorrect constructions more than correct ones.

mcq.q: What proportion of pair-construction acts were unassisted in 3-, 4- and 5-year-olds?
o: About 10%, 50%
About 90%, 50% and 10%
About 50%, 50% and 50%
mcq.e: "it takes 15 acts of pair construction to make a correct pyramid, and that more than 75% of these acts were unassisted among the 5-yr-olds, in contrast to 50% and 10% among the fours and threes."

mcq.q: Which kind of help did 3-year-olds receive most?
o: No help at all, because 3-year-olds needed no support from the tutor
General reminders of the task, median 12 times, more than at other ages
Direct intervention (showing), median 12 vs 6 at age 4 and 3 at age 5
Verbal correction, median 12 times, against 6 at age 4 and 3 at age 5
mcq.e: Table 1: Direct intervention (Showing) 12.0; 6.0; 3.0. Verbal correction 3.0; 5.0; 3.5.

mcq.q: What were the success rates of "showing" and "telling" for 3-year-olds?
o: Both 50%
Showing 40%, telling 18%
Showing 18%, telling 40%
Showing 80%, telling 57%

mcq.q: How many construction operations per tutor intervention were there in the three age groups?
o: 2.5; 1.8; 1.3 (increasing age)
mcq.e: Table 3: total operations 262/352/280; total interventions 201/198/112. Older children do more between interventions.

mcq.q: What proportion of 478 opportunities did the tutor follow her pre-set rules?
o: 100%, at every age (the tutor never broke her rules)
86%, most with 3-year-olds (92%)
30%, most often with 5-year-olds (least with 3-year-olds)
50%, the same at every age (each group had an equal rate)
mcq.e: Most "errors" with 4-year-olds were offering more help than the rules allowed (27 of 36 cases).

mcq.q: Why was the 4-year-old group hardest for fixed tutoring rules?
o: 4-year-olds were the noisiest and so hardest to keep on task
4-year-olds did not understand the task and needed it explained repeatedly
4-year-olds were the least cooperative and often refused to take part
"Try it and see" behaviour is unstructured, child-initiated
mcq.e: The middle phase is "disordered"; both learner and tutor are "at sea", so individualized teaching is hard to realize at the most critical point.

mcq.q: Which two theories must an effective tutor have?
o: A theory of language, and a theory of memory
A theory of age, and a theory of gender
A theory of reward and punishment, and a theory of motivation
A theory of the task and how to complete it
mcq.e: Without both, the tutor can neither generate feedback nor devise situations in which feedback fits this tutee at this point.

mcq.q: What are the six scaffolding functions in Wood et al.?
o: Praising, criticizing, ignoring, waiting, delaying, ending
Grading, ranking, rewarding, punishing, reminding, recording
Recruitment, reduction in degrees of freedom
Reading, writing, speaking, listening, doing, remembering
mcq.e: Recruitment, reduction in degrees of freedom, direction maintenance, marking critical features, frustration control, demonstration.

mcq.q: What is "recruitment"?
o: Recruiting more children to take part in the study across the city
Recruiting more tutors to work with a larger number of children
Enlisting the problem solver's interest in
Selecting the wooden blocks that would go into the box for the session
mcq.e: The tutor's first task; here it often meant weaning children from imaginative play with the blocks.

mcq.q: What is "reduction in degrees of freedom"?
o: Reducing the number of children in a group so the tutor can care for each child
Shortening sessions so the children do not tire and lose focus
Reducing the number of blocks in the box so children choose more easily
Simplifying the task by cutting the constituent acts
mcq.e: The tutor fills in the rest and lets the learner perfect the sub-routines he can manage; after N. Bernstein (1967) on cutting alternative movements in skill acquisition.

mcq.q: What is "direction maintenance"?
o: Keeping one fixed way of doing things so the child is not confused
Keeping the child seated at the table until the pyramid is finished
Keeping the pace of work fast so the child is not distracted
Keeping the learner in pursuit of the objective
mcq.e: Some children built pairs endlessly and would not move on to a flat quadruple: past success distracted from the ultimate goal.

mcq.q: What is "marking critical features"?
o: The tutor writes notes for parents
The tutor marks blocks with coloured pens
The tutor accentuates relevant features
The tutor grades with marks
mcq.e: It gives information about the discrepancy between what the child produced and what he would recognize as correct.

mcq.q: What principle does "frustration control" state?
o: Problem solving should be less stressful
Problem solving must be stressful to be remembered
The tutor must be strict
Children must not make errors
mcq.e: It may be done by "face saving" for errors or exploiting the wish to please; the important thing is to avoid too much dependency on the tutor.

mcq.q: What does "demonstration" mean in the paper?
o: Only reading the written instructions aloud without making the model first
Not merely performing before the child but "idealizing" the act
Only pointing at the wooden blocks that need to be joined without a word
Only showing an illustrative video to the child before the session starts
mcq.e: The tutor "imitates" in idealized form an attempted solution, expecting the learner to "imitate" it back more appropriately.

mcq.q: What does the study reveal about imitation?
o: Children never imitate the tutor in any situation during the sessions
Children imitate everything the tutor does, including new and unfamiliar actions
Children imitate purely mechanically, with no need to grasp what the action means
Children imitate only what they can already do fairly well
mcq.e: "there was not a single instance of what might be called 'blind matching behaviour'."

mcq.q: Why does the tutor "wither away" with older children?
o: Because older children dislike tutors
Because the child grasps the task
Because the blocks are too easy for older children
Because the tutor is tired
mcq.e: The tutor's role shifts from lure (age 3) to verbal prodder and corrector (age 4) to confirmer (age 5).

mcq.q: Which condition of the task do Wood et al. themselves name as limiting the conclusions?
o: The task had no structure at all
The task was fun, multifaceted
The task was used only with adults
The task was too hard for all children
mcq.e: "Note at the outset, then, that we have already constrained our results by the choice of a particular task."

mcq.q: How is scaffolding first defined in Wood's paper?
o: The adult doing the whole task for the child so the child finishes quickly
The adult giving orders one step at a time and the child simply obeying
The adult grading the child's work after the child has completed it
The adult "controlling" elements of the task beyond the learner's capacity
mcq.e: The aim is not only assisted completion but competence developing at a pace that outstrips unassisted efforts.

mcq.q: When designing a programming class with AI using cognitive apprenticeship, what should "modeling" be?
o: The instructor only grades the final product that students hand in
AI prints complete code that students copy straight into their submission
The instructor (or AI) thinks aloud while solving: predicting
Students watch a video of finished code running and copy it line by line
mcq.e: This is a design inference from the definition of modeling ("externalization of usually internal processes"), not an experimental result.

mcq.q: A Socratic AI model (hints instead of code) fits which concept?
o: Unproductive success: high short-term performance
Knowledge telling: listing ideas in order
Direct instruction: full teaching first
Scaffolding with fading: just enough support
mcq.e: Wood 1976: reduce degrees of freedom, mark critical features and control dependency; Collins 1991: "students get as much support as they need... but no more."

mcq.q: What main risk of AI scaffolding follows from Wood et al.?
o: Creating too much dependency on the tutor (AI)
The AI always answers wrongly so students end up learning incorrect content
The AI does not know the student's language so it cannot support them
The AI answers too slowly so students lose focus while they wait each time
mcq.e: Wood: "The major risk is in creating too much dependency on the tutor." That is why the thesis needs an explicit fading design.

mcq.q: Asking students to explain how the exercise works and write a reflection corresponds to which methods?
o: Exploration: students choose and pursue their own extension problems
Modeling: the instructor performs the whole task while students watch
Articulation and reflection
Coaching: the instructor watches students and reminds them of each mistake
mcq.e: Articulation: stating knowledge and reasoning; reflection: comparing one's process with an expert's or a peer's.

mcq.q: Letting students choose extension topics after mastery corresponds to which method?
o: Scaffolding: the instructor supports every step so students never make errors
Coaching: the instructor watches and reminds students of each mistake
Modeling: the instructor performs the whole task alone in front of the class
Exploration: fading in both problem solving and problem setting
mcq.e: Exploration is "the natural culmination of the fading of supports."

mcq.q: What is the most cautious conclusion when applying Wood 1976 to university programming?
o: It applies only to block puzzles
It is a theoretical suggestion
It cannot be used as a theoretical basis at all
It has been firmly proved for programming
mcq.e: The original authors stress that results are constrained by the task and sample.

essay.q: Explain what cognitive apprenticeship is and the three things to do to move from traditional apprenticeship to cognitive apprenticeship.
essay.m: Hint: an instructional model that brings apprenticeship into school to make thinking visible (Collins, Brown, Holum 1991). Three things: (1) identify the processes of the task and make them visible to students (and the students' thinking to the teacher); (2) situate abstract tasks in authentic contexts; (3) vary situations and articulate common aspects for transfer. State the four original elements: modeling, scaffolding, fading, coaching.

essay.q: Present the four-dimension framework (content, method, sequence, sociology) with a programming example for each dimension.
essay.m: Hint: Content: syntax and algorithms (domain), heuristics (try a small case), control strategies (change direction when stuck), learning strategies. Method: the six methods. Sequence: global first (a running program), complexity and diversity increasing. Sociology: real projects, community of practice (code review), intrinsic motivation, group work. The examples are design inferences, not experimental results.

essay.q: Compare Wood, Bruner and Ross's (1976) scaffolding with how AI supports students writing code; name which functions AI does well and which are easy to miss.
essay.m: Hint: six functions: recruitment, reduction in degrees of freedom, direction maintenance, marking critical features, frustration control, demonstration. AI easily does demonstration and marking; easily misses direction maintenance (keeping the learning goal, not just finishing), recruitment and control of dependency (it easily creates heavy dependence). Comprehension precedes production: students must recognize a correct solution first; AI may supply solutions beyond their understanding.

essay.q: Explain "situated cognition" and "authentic activity" (Brown, Collins, Duguid 1989), and give an "ersatz" programming task and a way to make it more authentic.
essay.m: Hint: knowledge is in part a product of the activity, context and culture; authentic activity is the ordinary practice of the culture. An ersatz task: write a factorial function just to submit it; more authentic: fix a bug or add a feature to a small open-source project, review a peer's code. Note the risk of "hybrid activity": implicitly framed by classroom culture but attributed to programmers' culture.

essay.q: State what you learn from the Weight Watchers and Schoenfeld examples about how experts and ordinary people solve problems, and apply it to teaching debugging.
essay.m: Hint: the dieter used the environment (cup, board, knife) as part of the calculation; the expert thinks aloud even in failure (Schoenfeld). Teaching debugging: the instructor live-codes, voices hypotheses, prints values, narrows the scope and shows dead ends openly; then a postmortem (abstracted replay) extracts general strategies; students rotate as producer and critic.

essay.q: Evaluate the limits of the evidence in Collins, Brown and Holum (1991) and Wood (1976) and say how you would test it in your own study.
essay.m: Hint: Collins 1991 is a synthesis; the reciprocal-teaching figures (15 to 85%, 30 to 80%, 40 to 80%) come from other studies and are not randomized experiments reported in detail; Wood 1976 describes 30 children without testing a hypothesis. Test: quasi-experiment or RCT (Module 13), measure performance without AI, measure dependence, and log the level of support over time to show fading.
